title: Quantum SWITCH-induced non-Markovianity is not entirely quantum
abstract: Indefinite causal order extends quantum information processing beyond fixed causal structures, with the quantum SWITCH serving as its canonical realization. By coherently superposing different orders of quantum channels, the quantum SWITCH has been shown to provide operational advantages in communication, computation, metrology, and related tasks. Despite these advances, the physical resources responsible for these advantages remains unclear. Recent studies have further revealed that the quantum SWITCH can generate memory effects, manifested as non-Markovian information backflow. In this work, we examine the origin of such memory and determine whether they reflect genuine (quantum) non-Markovianity or instead arises from classical origin. To this end, we analyze two representative scenarios: one based on discrete-time evolution and another formulated through dynamical maps in open quantum systems. We show that the memory effects generated by the quantum SWITCH are not genuinely quantum non-Markovian, thereby prompting a re-examination of the source of quantum advantage in indefinite causal order frameworks.
summary: This paper investigates the memory effects generated by the quantum SWITCH, a mechanism enabling indefinite causal order. By employing advanced diagnostics comparing standard and extended mutual information, the authors demonstrate that any observed non-Markovianity is not genuinely quantum. This forces a critical re-examination of which physical resources truly provide quantum advantages in such protocols.
main_problem: The study aims to determine if memory effects (non-Markovianity) generated by the quantum SWITCH are genuinely quantum or merely artifacts arising from classical correlations.
main_result: The research concludes that the observed memory effects in the quantum SWITCH dynamics are not genuinely quantum non-Markovian, suggesting a re-evaluation of the physical resources underpinning indefinite causal order advantages.
method: The authors analyze two scenarios (discrete and continuous time) using advanced diagnostics like CP-divisibility and comparing standard mutual information ($I(R; Q)$) against an extended environment mutual information ($I(R; QF)$).
model_or_system: The core model is the quantum SWITCH, which implements indefinite causal order by coherently superposing different orders of quantum channels acting on a system coupled to a control qubit.
key_observables: Non-Markovian information backflow, Quantum Mutual Information $I(R; Q)$, and the extended mutual information $I(R; QF)$.
important_parameters: The analysis distinguishes between genuine quantum non-Markovianity (requiring specific monotonicity in $I(R; QF)$) and classical sources of memory.
main_assumptions: The primary diagnostic tool relies on the assumption that true quantum non-Markovianity must manifest as a monotonic decrease when the environment is extended with an inert system ($F$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between $I(R; Q)$ (showing non-monotonic revival) and $I(R; QF)$ (showing monotonic decay) for both discrete and continuous time settings, confirming the classical origin of apparent memory.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the quantum SWITCH in both discrete-time evolution and continuous-time dynamical maps. The core logic involves applying various non-Markovianity measures and ultimately using the extended environment diagnostic ($F$) to distinguish genuine quantum effects from classical ones.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant for theoretical physicists working on open quantum systems because it provides a rigorous, advanced diagnostic tool (the $I(R; QF)$ test) to filter out spurious non-Markovian signatures that might otherwise lead to overestimation of quantum advantages in complex protocols like indefinite causal order.
